archetype.name: Retooling (offense-carried, defense still broken)
archetype.definition: A team two years removed from a 12-win season whose quarterback keeps the offense near league average, but whose defense has stayed among the league's worst for a second straight year, leaving a roster that needs real repair rather than a few breaks.

report.headline: Winning the turnover battle and still losing: the defense is the problem
report.take:
Washington is 1-4-1 with a -40 point differential, and the record is not much of an accident. The point differential implies about 2.1 wins, and winsOverExpected (-0.57) says the Commanders have been only slightly unlucky. The play-by-play ranks match the scoreboard: net EPA ranks 25th, the offense is 18th and the defense allowing EPA is 26th. This is a below-average team that has played like one, with one wrinkle that makes it worse than it looks.

That wrinkle is the ball. Washington has given it away only twice in six games against eight takeaways, a +6 margin that ranks third in the league per game. Turnover margin is the most reliable source of unearned wins in football, and this team has had it and still won once. Last year's team ranked 30th in turnover differential per game; this year's has been near the top of the league, and the record still hasn't improved. When the bounces even out, the scoring margin has room to get worse.

The main problem is the same as in 2025: the defense. Last season it ranked 31st in EPA allowed, and it hasn't recovered. Pass EPA allowed ranks 27th, success rate allowed 28th, and the red zone is the worst in the league, with opponents scoring touchdowns on 81.8% of trips. Offenses know where to attack. Washington faces the league's strongest pass funnel (opponents pass 7.2 points more often than expected), and tight ends have feasted, with TE1s scoring 9.1 PPR points a game over their average, last in the league. Seattle's 25th-ranked offense threw for 393 yards on them. The run defense is respectable and almost never allows the explosive run, but that mostly pushes opponents toward the passing game, where they are getting results.

The offense is roughly what you'd expect from Jayden Daniels with a shaky line. It is close to neutral by EPA, with good running lanes (3.21 yards before contact, 3rd) undone by pressure: the line ranks 28th in pressure rate allowed and gave up five and four sacks the last two weeks. The one Marcus Mariota start was the low point, 13-30 with -9.5 passing EPA, so Daniels' health matters a lot. Now Terry McLaurin is gone for the year with a torn patellar tendon. Stefon Diggs already led the team in targets, but a passing game that ranked 19th in EPA just lost its second option. That makes a turnaround harder.

strengths.title: Ball security and opportunistic takeaways
strengths.body: Washington has turned it over only twice and taken it away eight times, a margin that ranks third per game. Part of it is real: Daniels has avoided giveaways and the pass rush has a decent pressure rate. But a margin like this almost always shrinks, and a 2025 team that ranked 30th in the same stat is a reminder of how quickly it can turn.

strengths.title: Run lanes are there
strengths.body: The line opens holes before contact better than almost anyone, at 3.21 yards before contact (3rd), and converts 75% of short-yardage tries. When it works, as in the 202-yard rushing day against the Giants, it carries the offense. Run EPA still ranks only 21st, so the backs aren't adding much after first contact. This is something to build on, but it doesn't yet produce efficient offense.

strengths.title: Run defense kills explosives
strengths.body: Opponents almost never break a long run on Washington; its explosive-run rate allowed ranks 2nd, and short passes are well defended (7th). The front is sound at the line of scrimmage. The catch is that this is why teams throw on them so often, and deep shots are where the defense breaks.

concerns.title: Pass defense and red zone collapse
concerns.body: Pass EPA allowed ranks 27th, deep-ball EPA allowed 22nd, and opponents finish 81.8% of red-zone trips with touchdowns, worst in the league. Tight ends have been the biggest problem. This is the second straight year the defense has ranked near the bottom, so treat it as structural rather than a slow start. Expect points allowed to stay high.

concerns.title: Protection breaking down, McLaurin gone
concerns.body: The line ranks 28th in pressure rate and 27th in QB hit rate allowed, and it gave up nine sacks over the last two games. Losing McLaurin for the season removes the passing game's second target. Diggs and Antonio Williams now have to carry it behind a line that can't hold up long. Passing efficiency is more likely to drop than rise.

concerns.title: Special teams giving away field
concerns.body: Special teams have cost about 1.57 EPA a game (26th), adding short fields to a defense that already can't stop anyone in the red zone. Combined with turnover luck that should fade, close games are more likely to go the wrong way.

trend.note: The results have swung widely: a near-upset at Philadelphia, a blowout in Dallas, a shootout win over Seattle, a no-show with Mariota, a tie with the Giants and a cover at San Francisco. The offense rises and falls with Daniels and the run game, while the pass protection has steadily gotten worse.

nextGame.headline: Rested Washington hosts a depleted, sputtering Eagles offense
nextGame.body:
Washington comes off a bye with 13 days of rest and is a 4.5-point favorite at home against a 2-5 Philadelphia team that has covered only one of six. The Eagles' offense ranks 30th in EPA and 31st in yards per game, and their run game gets stuffed on 30.2% of carries, worst in the league. Their defense is weak in exactly the places Washington needs help. Philadelphia ranks 31st in rush EPA allowed, and its pass rush is among the league's weakest by sacks (29th) and last in QB hit rate. That relieves Washington's biggest problem, pass protection. The first meeting was a two-point Philadelphia win in Week 1, and the low total of 40.5 points to a grind.

Availability favors Washington. Philadelphia is listed without tackle Lane Johnson and center Jake Majors, both full-time starters, along with receivers DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks, edge Nolan Smith Jr. and corner Michael Carter II, and Saquon Barkley is questionable with back and hamstring trouble. Jalen Hurts started last week after Tanner McKee filled in for Week 6. Washington loses McLaurin for the year, and DT Javon Kinlaw and DE Charles Omenihu are questionable up front. Mariota is only the backup, so Daniels' health is what matters at quarterback.

waysToWin.title: Run at the league's softest front
waysToWin.body: Philadelphia ranks 31st in rush EPA allowed, and Washington's line creates yards before contact as well as almost anyone. A heavy dose of Croskey-Merritt and White keeps a shorthanded offense ahead of the chains and shortens the game, which suits the favorite. The Giants game showed what this looks like when the lanes stay open.

waysToWin.title: Clean pockets for Daniels
waysToWin.body: The Eagles rank 29th in sacks and last in QB hit rate, and Nolan Smith Jr. is out. Washington's protection has been its weak spot, and this is the friendliest pass rush it has seen in weeks. Philadelphia has also let WR1s score 4 PPR points a game over their average, which sets up Diggs as the new focal point.

waysToWin.title: Pressure a patched-up line
waysToWin.body: Washington's pass rush ranks 9th in pressure rate, and Philadelphia's line was already allowing pressure on 26.3% of dropbacks before losing Johnson and Majors. Philadelphia's offense ranks 30th in EPA and is missing its top receivers. Forcing passing downs could produce long stalled drives rather than the shootout Washington's secondary can't survive.

waysToLose.title: Red-zone leaks and field position
waysToLose.body: Washington allows touchdowns on a league-worst share of red-zone trips, and Philadelphia's special teams (6th) are strong where Washington's (26th) are weak. A weak offense doesn't need many long drives if it keeps starting near midfield and then scores touchdowns instead of kicking field goals.

waysToLose.title: Passing game stalls without McLaurin
waysToLose.body: With McLaurin out, Diggs, Williams, Okonkwo and Burks have to carry a passing game that ranks 19th in EPA. If Philadelphia commits to stopping Diggs and the run stalls, Washington could struggle to move the ball in a low-scoring game, and it would have to win close, which it has done only 37.5% of the time.

waysToLose.title: Eagles' aggression on fourth down
waysToLose.body: Philadelphia has gone for it on every fourth down it was tracked on (1st), and Washington allows 44.4% on third down (25th). A defense that gives up conversions can let a bad offense extend drives and control the game, which is how the Week 1 meeting got close.

nextGame.watch: Whether Washington's run game can push around the league's 31st-ranked run defense early. If it does, the weak Eagles offense has to play from behind, which it isn't built for.

restOfSeason.body:
The remaining schedule has soft spots: road trips to Tennessee and Arizona and home games with Houston and Atlanta. It also has hard ones: Minnesota's top-ranked defense, Cincinnati, Jacksonville, and Dallas's 4th-ranked offense. A team ranked 25th in net EPA should split games like these at best. Expect the turnover margin to drift back toward even, which removes the one thing that has kept scores close. Losing McLaurin should take a little off a passing game that was already only average. The defense has ranked near the bottom two years running, so don't expect a sudden fix. Points allowed should drop slightly from 28.7 as schedule and red-zone luck even out, but not by much.

What holds up is the run blocking, the run defense and Daniels' ball security. What likely gets worse is the takeaway rate and the scoring margin that rests on it. A finish around .400 is reasonable. Playoff contention would require the pass defense to improve sharply, and nothing in the profile points that way.
swingFactors: Daniels staying healthy behind a leaky line
Any improvement in red-zone and tight-end defense

confidence.note: Six games, one missed Daniels start, and McLaurin's loss changes the offense; but the defensive issues match last season.
